newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin in good form as heart operation nears.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin in good form as heart operation nears.

text.p: Doctors said on Monday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin was in fine form as the clock ticked away to his planned heart operation.

A doctors' statement released by the Kremlin said Yeltsin's temperature and blood pressure were normal. But the specialists gave no date for the bypass operation, which will improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart.
"B.N. Yeltsin's health is completely satisfactory," the brief statement said. "The preparations for the operation are practically over."
Russian news agencies said the head of the Russian Orthodox Church had prayed for Yeltsin.

"Heal the illnesses, the spiritual and corporeal ailments of the president of our Russian land, forgive him his transgressions witting and unwitting, deliver him soon from his sickbed and restore him to good health," Patriarch Alexiy said.

Yeltsin, breaking with a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of its leaders, said on September 5 he would have an operation on his heart and doctors said later that month that it would take 6-10 weeks to prepare him for surgery.
Yeltsin's absence from the Kremlin -- he has spent only a few days there since winning a second term in office in July -- brought a simmering power struggle out into the open.
The Kremlin's relations with the communist-dominated parliament are poor and the opposition says chief of staff Anatoly Chubais is seizing too much power.
Financial markets are watching closely -- dealers say a successful operation could point to stability in Russia and increase chances of an investment boom.
Doctors have treated Yeltsin for blood and thyroid problems and he looked healthy in recent television appearances.
The Kremlin said Russian specialist Renat Akchurin would lead the team carrying out the operation.
The team includes pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Micheal DeBakey, although the U.S. specialist will not wield the surgeon's knife. He said last week he expected doctors to operate early this week.

Yeltsin has already handed some powers over to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who will deputise during the operation and who chaired a meeting of the influential Security Council in Moscow on Monday.
The council, normally chaired by the president, groups senior Russian ministers and security officials.

The Kremlin has made clear Yeltsin will give Chernomyrdin control of Russia's nuclear arsenal just before the surgery. A second decree to be signed after Yeltsin comes out of the anaesthetic will annul this -- if all goes according to plan.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and concern about his health has overshadowed the political and economic scene since he defeated Communist Party candidate Gennady Zyuganov on July 3 to win a second term in the Kremlin.

Zyuganov's communists have kept a low profile in the State Duma lower house of parliament, where they are the largest party. But their candidates have done well in many of the local elections being held across Russia.

The local polls allow voters to choose a new regional governor, but are important on a national level because the regional governors also become members of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.
A communist-backed candidate will represent the remote northeastern region of Magadan, location of many of Soviet-era dictator Josef Stalin's prison camps after polls on Sunday.
A second vote, in the northwestern region of Pskov, was won by the candidate representing Vladimir Zhirinovsky's extreme nationalist Liberal Democratic Party.

Senior presidential aide Alexander Kazakov, expressing the Kremlin's unease over the whole system of elected governors, told a news conference on Monday it was preparing measures to rein in influential regional leaders.
